# Transcaval Access for Structural Heart Interventions: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Transfemoral arterial access is the established default route for transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), but it cannot be used in a meaningful minority of patients. Although the transfemoral approach is the preferred vascular access for TAVR, it may be unfeasible in approximately 5%-10% of patients owing to anatomic challenges such as small vessel size, marked vessel tortuosity, or extensive calcification of the iliofemoral vasculature [1]. Historically, alternatives have included transthoracic (transapical and transaortic) routes, but transthoracic access is inferior compared with femoral-artery access, perhaps in part because of the clinical features precluding femoral artery access [2]. Against this background, transcaval access has emerged as a fully percutaneous, nonfemoral alternative for delivering large-bore devices to the abdominal aorta [3].

## Concept and rationale

Caval-aortic access entails delivering large vascular sheaths into the abdominal aorta via the femoral vein through the inferior vena cava (IVC) [4]. Counterintuitive as it seems, the technique exploits favorable retroperitoneal physiology: although counterintuitive, its relative safety derives from the recognition that interstitial hydraulic pressure exceeds venous pressure, so arterial bleeding harmlessly decompresses into the nearby caval venous hole [3]. The concept was first validated preclinically: in 2013, Halabi et al published a preclinical study performing transcaval access to aorta in 14 swine with successfully fistula occlusion and survival in all 14 specimens [5]. In that work, the guidewire was connected to an electrosurgery pencil using hemostats and energized for 1-2 seconds in "cutting mode" for crossing [5]. This electrosurgical traversal principle was later formalized as a distinct discipline of transcatheter electrosurgery [6].

## Technique and planning

The procedure begins with venous and target preparation. A technique of transfemoral venous access for retrograde TAVR was developed by entering the abdominal aorta through the adjoining inferior vena cava, with transcaval access obtained over an electrified guidewire directed from the inferior vena cava toward a snare in the abdominal aorta [7]. The resulting fistula is then closed: transcaval access to the aorta allows transcatheter aortic valve replacement in patients without other good access options, and the resulting aorto-caval fistula is closed with a nitinol cardiac occluder device [8].

Meticulous computed tomography (CT) planning is central to safety. The crossing target must have a calcium-free window on the right wall of the abdominal aorta, close to the vena cava, free of interposed structures such as bowel or lymph nodes, and away from branches that could be obstructed by a closure device, such as right renal arteries and left renal veins or the aortic bifurcation [9]. Dedicated CT planning methodology has been described in detail [10], and the technical "how-to" of access and closure has been published as practical guidance [11]. Contemporary best-practice consensus emphasizes that targets need to be sufficiently far (approximately ≥10-15 mm) from important aortic branches to allow bailout covered stents a hemostatic landing zone seal without branch occlusion [12]. The same document notes that bailout covered stents will usually occlude the inferior mesenteric artery, so patency of the celiac and superior mesenteric arteries should be checked during planning, lest covered stent implantation cause mesenteric ischemia [12].

## Clinical evidence in TAVR

The first human series was reported in 2014. Between July 2013 and January 2014, 19 patients underwent TAVR via caval-aortic access; caval-aortic access and tract closure was successful in all 19, and TAVR was successful in 17 [13]. A prospective, multicenter NHLBI investigational device exemption trial followed, enrolling 100 subjects [14]. All TAVR procedures were successful, and 30-day landmark survival was 92% [14]. One-year follow-up confirmed durability of healed tracts [15], and an accompanying editorial framed these intermediate-term outcomes favorably [16].

European experience has corroborated feasibility. In a five-center registry, transcaval access was successful in 49 out of 50 patients and closure of the caval-aortic puncture site with a nitinol cardiac occluder was successful in all cases without need for emergent surgery [17]. A propensity-weighted comparison against supra-aortic access found favorable signals: the stroke/transient ischemic attack rates were 3% for transcaval TAVR and 13% for transaxillary TAVR [18], an analysis discussed in an accompanying editorial [19]. A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis of 8 studies (467 patients) reported that transcaval TAVR procedures achieved a success rate of 98.5%, with a 30-day all-cause mortality rate of 6.1%, and postoperative stroke or TIA, major vascular complications, and major or life-threatening bleeding occurring in 3.3%, 8.7%, and 7.5% of cases, respectively [20]. A device-traversal variant has also been described for patients with surgical grafts: there is no prior experience traversing a synthetic aortic graft, but successful traversal of a polyester aortic graft using radiofrequency energy applied from the tip of a guidewire allowed retrograde TAVR from a femoral vein [21], later extended to a sheathless approach through an aortic graft [22].

## Applications beyond TAVR

Transcaval access is now used more broadly. Transcaval access has been performed in thousands of patients for transcatheter aortic valve replacement and endovascular thoracic aneurysm repair and to avoid limb ischemia in percutaneous mechanical circulatory support [12]. For thoracic endovascular aortic repair (TEVAR), the first human application showed that TEVAR was successfully performed, followed by intervascular tract occlusion, and at 1 month the aneurysm was free of endoleaks and the aortocaval tract had healed [23], with subsequent confirmatory reports [24]. The route also enables high-output mechanical circulatory support: all ten patients underwent emergency implantation of the 7 mm diameter Impella 5.0 device via transcaval access, demonstrating feasibility for emergency nonsurgical implantation in cardiogenic shock with small or diseased iliofemoral arteries [25]. The Impella 5.x specifically requires transcaval or surgical transfemoral, transaxillary, or transsubclavian placement [26]. It has additionally been applied in transcatheter treatment of subaortic stenosis [27] and combined with adjunctive techniques such as BASILICA to prevent coronary obstruction [28].

## Limitations and future directions

A principal barrier has been device availability: the dissemination of transcaval access and closure techniques has been hampered by the unavailability of commercially marketed devices [12]. Closure currently relies on off-label nitinol occluders, although a dedicated closure device has progressed to first-in-human testing [29]. Importantly, available evidence derives from highly experienced centers, and a proctored, programmatic approach is advised, given the expertise required in caval-aortic puncture, electrocautery, and closure [30]. Overall, transcaval access has matured from a counterintuitive bailout into a credible alternative-access strategy, though randomized comparative data and purpose-built closure devices remain priorities.
